prompt:
Write an essay of about 1,500 words on whether primary schools should still teach joined-up handwriting. Take a side and argue for it.

Write it as plain prose with no headings or lists.

Write it in this voice: Calm, even register. Mostly medium-length, complete sentences, with length set by content rather than rhythm. No pattern of a short hook paid off by a longer sentence. Plain words over writerly ones, and lines allowed to sit flat. Numbers, names and concrete facts carry the point instead of abstractions. Em dashes, parentheticals, adverbs, doublets and parallelism kept rare. Descriptive writing states what a thing is and does, and any view is labelled as a view. British spelling.

text:
Primary schools should keep teaching joined-up handwriting. The case does not rest on nostalgia, and it does not require a belief that children will spend their adult lives writing letters by hand. It rests on a narrower point. For the next decade or more, most children in English schools will write by hand for a large part of each school day, and they will sit their most important exams with a pen. A skill that is used that much is worth teaching properly, and a joined hand, taught plainly and without fuss, is the form that serves most children best. I will argue that the subject should stay in the curriculum, that it should be taught from about the age of seven, and that it should be treated as a practical skill and not as a test of neatness.

The present position is mixed. In England the national curriculum, in force since 2014, asks pupils in Year 2 to start using some of the strokes needed to join letters. In Years 3 and 4 they are expected to use joins and to know which pairs of letters are better left unjoined. Other countries have moved away from this. Finland removed compulsory cursive from its national core curriculum in 2016, and its schools now give more time to typing. In the United States the Common Core standards of 2010 left cursive out, and many districts stopped teaching it. Since then a number of states have put it back, and by most counts more than twenty now require it in some form. California did so in 2023 for pupils in grades one to six. School systems that take education seriously have reached different answers, so the question is open.

The strongest argument against joined writing is that time is limited. A school day has a fixed length, and every minute given to joins is a minute not given to reading, number work or typing. Most adults type more than they write, and a child who learns to touch type early may produce text faster and more legibly than one with a weak hand. Print letters are also easier to learn, because they look like the letters in books. Some studies suggest that children taught a simple italic or print style write about as fast as those taught a looped cursive. I accept most of this. It is a good reason to teach joins economically and to drop the looped, ornamental styles that older schemes used. It is not a good reason to drop joins altogether.

The first reason to keep them is that handwriting remains the main way pupils show what they know. Most GCSE and A level papers in England are written by hand, and many run for two hours. An examiner cannot give marks for an answer that cannot be read, and a candidate who writes slowly cannot fit in what they know. The same is true earlier in school. A study by McHale and Cermak, carried out in the United States and published in 1992, observed primary classrooms and found that pupils spent between 31 and 60 per cent of the school day on fine motor tasks, most of them with pencil and paper. Whatever the long-term future of handwriting, it is the daily medium of the primary classroom now. Laptops and tablets are spreading, but they are not yet in every pupil's hands in every lesson, and many schools do not want them there.

The second reason is fluency. A child who has to think about how to form each letter has less attention left for what to say. In a 1997 study, Steve Graham, Virginia Berninger and their colleagues tested pupils in the first three years of primary school and found that handwriting and spelling skills explained a substantial share of the differences in the length and quality of their compositions. This is a finding about handwriting in general and not about joins in particular, and I do not want to claim more than it shows. The point is that when a hand is slow and effortful, the writing suffers, and the pupil often writes less and says less than they could. Automatic letter formation is a means to better writing, and schools should aim for it.

There is also some evidence that writing by hand helps learning, though it is less settled than its supporters suggest. Longcamp and colleagues reported in 2005 that young children who copied letters by hand later recognised them better than children who typed them. Mueller and Oppenheimer found in 2014 that students who took lecture notes by hand did better on conceptual questions than those who typed, but later attempts to repeat the result have had mixed outcomes. I would not build the argument on this evidence. I would say only that it points the same way as common experience, which is that handwriting is not a skill we can drop without any cost.

That leaves the case for joining, as opposed to printing. It is the weakest part of the argument, and I will state it as it stands. A joined hand has fewer pen lifts. Each lift breaks the movement and forces a small decision about where the next letter starts. When a word is written in one movement, the hand learns common letter strings such as ing, ed and tion as units, and some teachers believe this helps spelling. That is a view, and the evidence for it is thin. The evidence on speed is also mixed, with some studies finding that joined writers are faster in the upper years of primary and secondary school and others finding no difference. What I can say is that pupils tend to develop a joined or semi-joined hand by the age of eleven or twelve whether or not anyone teaches it. Children who are not taught tend to invent their own forms, and these are often slow, awkward or hard to read. A taught set of joins gives them a sound starting point, and they can adapt it as they please later.

Teachers who work with children with dyslexia or dyspraxia often favour joined writing from the start, on the grounds that the continuous movement is easier to remember than a series of separate marks. That is also a view, and children differ. But it does suggest that the benefit of a taught system may be greatest for those who find writing hardest. A child from a home with few books and no keyboard depends on school to teach this skill, and a child who finds it difficult needs a clear method more than a confident one does. Dropping the subject would not affect every pupil equally.

A smaller point concerns reading. Handwritten cards, letters and notes, and a great many historical documents, are written in joined script. A child who has never seen it taught will find them hard to read. The US National Archives has asked for volunteers to help transcribe handwritten records, in part because fewer people can read them. Few children will need to read old documents, but many will receive a card from a grandparent, and being unable to read it is a small loss that costs almost nothing to avoid.

The cost of teaching joins is low. Ten minutes a day, five days a week, for thirty-six weeks is thirty hours a year. Spread over Years 2, 3 and 4, that is ninety hours out of well over three thousand hours of lessons across those years. Such lessons need not be dull, and they can be combined with spelling practice, which is where the claimed benefit for spelling would show up if it exists. A school could teach the four or five main groups of joins in a set order, accept that some letter pairs are better left apart, and stop grading pupils on neatness once they are legible and reasonably quick. By Year 5 or 6 the aim should be a hand the child can keep up for a whole exam paper. Nobody needs the copperplate of a Victorian clerk.

None of this is an argument against typing. Children should learn to type, and I would start formal keyboard lessons around Year 4 or 5. The two skills do different jobs, and a child who has both is better placed than one who has only one. The risk is that schools treat the choice as either-or, on the assumption that the keyboard has already won. It has not won in the classroom, and it has not won in the exam hall.

In the end the question is whether a modest, well-defined skill that pupils will use every day for years is worth a small part of the timetable. I think it is. The research does not prove that joined writing makes children cleverer, and I have tried not to pretend it does. It shows that fluent handwriting helps writing, that most school work and most formal exams still depend on it, and that children left to find their own way often find a worse one. Primary schools should keep teaching a joined hand, teach it briefly and simply, and then leave pupils to make it their own.
